title: Did Vikings Really Wear Horned Helmets?
hook: Close your eyes and picture a Viking. Chances are, you just gave him a helmet with horns.

segments.n: Here’s the problem: archaeologists have never found a Viking-age helmet with horns. Not one.
segments.p: A dig site with a shallow pit and a small flag, Hiro in a hat holding a magnifying glass over the ground, a large crossed-out horned helmet icon floating beside him colored amber-orange, pale earth tones. segments.n: The best-preserved helmet from that era, found in Gjermundbu, Norway, is simple, round, and has no horns at all.
segments.p: A museum display case holding a plain round iron helmet without horns on a small stand, the helmet colored amber-orange, a small blank placard, Hiro standing beside the case pointing at the helmet. segments.n: So where did it come from? Horned helmets were real, but from the Bronze Age, more than a thousand years earlier, and probably ceremonial.
segments.p: A Bronze Age hillside with a horned ceremonial helmet resting on a stand, the horns colored amber-orange, Hiro in a simple wrap looking up at it, a faint timeline arrow running behind him. segments.n: The look was popularized in the 1870s, when a costume designer added horns for Wagner’s operas.
segments.p: A theater stage with curtains and a spotlight, a costume designer figure holding a sketchbook and a horned helmet colored amber-orange, Hiro sitting in the audience seats watching. segments.n: A costume became history. So what else do you think you know about the past just because a picture stuck?
